beats.narration_text: Hello, this is Liam, in for Bear. Jay-Ann Yin's game is Lane Tactics: archers on a five-lane board, where you win by reaching the enemy's back row. This assignment adds particle effects: a burst where an arrow hits, and a trail behind the arrow in flight. The prompt on screen is an illustrative reconstruction.

shot.label: Illustrative reconstruction of the Claude interface — not a transcript

props.segment: A Hit Burst and an Arrow Trail
props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about Lane Tactics — archers on a five-lane board, simultaneous orders, win by reaching the enemy's back row — into two particle effects: a hit burst that shows which archer an arrow hit, and a trail that shows who shot whom. Test both, price both, and show me what a headless run cannot.

beats.role_note: walker B00: ClaudeComposerAsk; prompt begins 'Please use Walker to convert my game design document about'; illustrative reconstruction, labelled. Result lines are recorded numbers (TEST-REPORT A6.1).
beats.duration_note: voice 16.917s + lead 0.0s, padded with silence to 508 frames = 508/30 s

beats.narration_text: Two particle effects: a burst that marks the hit, and a trail that shows the shot. The tests guard every setting. How they look was decided by Jay-Ann's eyes, one revision at a time.

props.text:
Two particle effects for Lane Tactics:
a burst where the arrow lands,
a trail behind it in flight.
Tests decide how they look.

beats.role_note: walker B01: hesitant-writer summary; 'Tests decide' -> 'Jiean's eyes decide' is the film's point (settings are tested, the look was tuned by eye).

beats.duration_note: voice 10.496s + lead 0.8s, padded with silence to 384 frames = 384/30 s

beats.narration_text: Each effect has one job. Effect A: an arrow hit an archer, and which one. It fires on an event, every damaged event. Effect B: who shot whom, and along which path. It runs while a condition holds, an arrow in flight. One is a CPU particle node, one a GPU node. And the game runs on Godot's Compatibility renderer. That matters later.
beats.role_note: Setup: the two jobs, event vs condition, node types, renderer (CHANGE-BRIEF §1, §2; project.godot:25).
beats.duration_note: voice 18.411s + lead 0.0s, padded with silence to 571 frames = 571/30 s

beats.narration_text: Effect A is one scene: a root and three CPU particle nodes, Flash, Splinters and Dust. Here are the splinters. Line ninety-one: saved not emitting, so nothing fires when a scene loads. Fourteen, born all at once. Up to seventy-five degrees either side of straight up, at one hundred forty to two hundred sixty pixels a second, and gravity pulls them back down. Line ninety-eight: local coords off, so each splinter stays where it was born.

beats.narration_text: Nothing in this game sends a signal. So the driver runs every frame, right after the game's own update, and reads the list of events the game has played. Line forty-four: every new damaged event gets a burst. Line forty-nine: every emitter's speed scale is the game's speed, and zero while it's paused. The driver reads the game. It never writes it.

beats.narration_text: The flash wasn't planned like this. The brief gave it point one two seconds. Jay-Ann watched it in the game and wrote: I can barely realize it happens. So it was tuned, one setting per revision, with Claude's prediction written down before each edit. Lifetime, then size, then lifetime again. Line sixty-four now says one point oh eight seconds.

beats.narration_text: The trail's driver keeps one entry per arrow. While the arrow is in the game's list, the trail moves to its tip, with the game's own arc formula: line sixty-nine. On the frame the arrow leaves the list, both emitters stop, line seventy-four, and a countdown starts: the wisps' lifetime, seven tenths of a second of game time. Then the node is freed. A new arrow gets a new trail.

beats.narration_text: Now the tests. The configuration tests load each scene and read every value back against the brief: one hundred seven checks for the burst, one hundred thirty-five for the trail. This part reads the scene as plain text, line by line, looking for Godot three names, like initial velocity without its min. Why read the text? Because an old name might load without a word.

beats.narration_text: Jay-Ann tested the tests. Mutation one: write initial velocity, the Godot three name, on the splinters. The scene loaded with no error and no warning, and the value read back as zero. Two checks failed: the text scan and the read-back. In the game, Jay-Ann saw almost nothing wrong, only a flash that seemed to fade earlier. That's why it needs a test. Mutation two: one value changed, exactly one check failed.

beats.narration_text: The state tests play the game with real key presses at sixty frames a second, and check every frame against the rules. This check compares each trail's stop with the hit it leads to. The brief said: within one frame. The agent's first run measured zero, minus two, zero, zero, minus two. Up to two frames early.

beats.narration_text: The agent didn't widen the bound to make it pass. It left the check failing, and reported it. The brief was wrong, so the brief was corrected first, in a dated revision, and only then the test: thirty-one of thirty-one. Why two frames? The arrow's clock and the hit cue advance in different places. Game timing was out of scope, so that stays open. And no headless run draws a single particle.

beats.narration_text: Last, the process shader. Jay-Ann converted the wisps' material into a shader in the editor, and saved it unedited. Nearly five hundred lines, and the game doesn't use it. It's a particles shader: a start function for each new particle, and a process function for every step. Jay-Ann's table: shader type on line three, start on three twenty-three, process on three seventy-eight. The initial velocity is mixed from its minimum and maximum on two thirty-two. Gravity becomes the force on four twelve. Scale and colour over life are applied on two fifty-four and two fifty-five. And line four forty-one belongs to turbulence, which the wisps switch on.

beats.narration_text: Who did what. Jay-Ann chose both effects, their jobs and the retrigger rule, wrote every prediction, the budget and the six answers, ran the mutations, captured every strip, read the profiler, and judged every revision. Claude agents, working from the brief, wrote the scenes, the drivers, the tests and the price script; Claude Code reviewed them, made the tuning edits Jay-Ann asked for, and built the price fixture. Caught on the way: a bound in the brief that was wrong, a prediction that ignored draw order, and a cleanup loop that deleted a strip, which Jay-Ann captured again. No image files: the textures are gradients inside the scenes. Source shown: tag a6.
beats.role_note: Human and AI contributions (SOURCES.md A6), mistakes caught (FRICTIONAL A6, TUNING), textures.
beats.duration_note: voice 33.765s + lead 0.0s, padded with silence to 1031 frames = 1031/30 s

beats.narration_text: Verdict. Checked: every setting reads back, both mutations were caught, the rules held on every frame at sixty frames a second, two bursts overlap on a two-hit turn, and both effects cost a few thousandths of a millisecond, far under budget. Wrong: the brief's one-frame bound, Claude's first flash prediction, and Jay-Ann's price predictions, off by less than a hundredth of a millisecond. Uncertain: why the trail stops up to two frames early, what the profiler's four to six milliseconds with vsync on contain, and whether a hidden trail keeps simulating.
